claim: Female medaka under breeding (LD) condition eat more than those under non-breeding (SD) condition
source: We found that female medaka under the breeding (LD) condition eat more than those under the non-breeding (SD) condition (Figure 1B; p=0.02519).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from food intake assay shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance p=0.02519

claim: Male medaka show no significant difference in food intake between breeding and non-breeding conditions
source: In contrast to female, in males there was no significant difference in food intake between the breeding and non-breeding condition (Figure 1C; p=0.6540).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from food intake assay shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance p=0.6540

claim: agrp1 shows higher brain expression under breeding condition than under non-breeding condition in female medaka
source: Among the conventional candidate feeding-related neuropeptides, we identified two kinds of neuropeptides, agrp1 and npyb, both of which showed higher expression in LD than in SD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D

claim: npyb shows higher brain expression under breeding condition than under non-breeding condition in female medaka
source: Among the conventional candidate feeding-related neuropeptides, we identified two kinds of neuropeptides, agrp1 and npyb, both of which showed higher expression in LD than in SD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D

claim: AgRP and NPY have orexigenic effects mainly in mice
source: Both AgRP and NPY are known to have orexigenic effects mainly in mice (Schwartz et al., 2000; Andermann and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Schwartz et al., 2000; Andermann and Lowell, 2017)

claim: agrp1-expressing neurons are distributed in the nucleus ventralis tuberis (NVT) of the hypothalamus
source: The agrp1 neurons were distributed in the nucleus ventralis tuberis (NVT) of the hypothalamus (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: agrp2-expressing neurons are distributed in the telencephalon and in the hypothalamus
source: while agrp2 neurons were expressed in the telencephalon and in the hypothalamus (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C

claim: npya neurons are distributed widely from telencephalon to hypothalamus
source: On the other hand, npya neurons were distributed more widely from telencephalon to hypothalamus (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D

claim: npyb neurons are distributed locally in the nucleus ventralis telencephali pars dorsalis (Vd) of the telencephalon
source: npyb neurons were distributed locally in the nucleus ventralis telencephali pars dorsalis (Vd) of the telencephalon (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E

claim: agrp and npy are mostly co-expressed in hypothalamic neurons in mice
source: In mice, agrp is known to be only expressed in the hypothalamus and mostly co-expressed with npy (Hahn et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Hahn et al., 1998)

claim: agrp1 signals are not observed in npya neurons in medaka
source: In medaka, on the other hand, agrp1 signals were not observed in npya neurons (Figure 2F, left)
evidence: Supported by double in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F

claim: agrp2 signals are not observed in hypothalamic npya neurons in medaka
source: In addition, agrp2 signals were not observed in hypothalamic npya neurons (Figure 2F, right), either.
evidence: Supported by double in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F

claim: AgRP and NPY are not co-expressed in medaka
source: These results suggest that AgRP and NPY are not co-expressed in medaka.
evidence: Inferred from the double ISH results showing no co-localization of agrp1/agrp2 with npya

claim: 2-week food restriction increases agrp1 expression in female medaka
source: RT-qPCR analysis demonstrated that 2-week FR increased the expression of agrp1 (Figure 2G; p=0.001243)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G with statistical significance p=0.001243

claim: 2-week food restriction decreases npyb expression in female medaka
source: RT-qPCR analysis demonstrated that 2-week FR increased the expression of agrp1 (Figure 2G; p=0.001243) but decreased that of npyb (Figure 2J; p=0.0003108)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2J with statistical significance p=0.0003108

claim: agrp2 does not significantly change expression between Fed and FR conditions
source: On the other hand, agrp2 did not significantly change their expressions between Fed and FR conditions (Figure 2H; p=0.9551).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2H with statistical significance p=0.9551

claim: AgRP1, NPYa, and NPYb may be the 'feeding-related peptides' in female medaka
source: Thus, the results suggest that AgRP1, NPYa, and NPYb may be the 'feeding-related peptides' in female medaka.
evidence: Inferred from the expression changes of these peptides in response to food restriction

claim: agrp1 expression level is higher in LD than in SD female medaka by RT-qPCR
source: First, we performed whole-brain RT-qPCR and found that the expression level of agrp1 was higher in LD than in SD female (Figure 3A, p=0.001865).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance p=0.001865

claim: The number of agrp1-expressing neurons is larger in LD than in SD females
source: In ISH experiments, we observed larger number of agrp1-expressing neurons in LD than in SD females (Figure 3B and C; p=0.02828, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3B and C with statistical significance p=0.02828

claim: npyb expression is significantly higher in LD than in SD by RT-qPCR
source: On the other hand, npyb expression in RT-qPCR was significantly higher in LD than that in SD (Figure 3D; p=0.0001554)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance p=0.0001554

claim: npyb-expressing cell number is not significantly different between LD and SD
source: although ISH analysis demonstrated that npyb-expressing cell number was not significantly different between LD and SD (Figure 3E; p=0.4206).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance p=0.4206

claim: Higher expression of npyb under breeding condition may be due to increased expression in each neuron expressing npyb
source: These results suggest that the expression level for each neuron increased in LD compared with SD. Thus, higher expression of npyb under the breeding condition may be due to the increase of expressions in each neuron expressing npyb.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that total npyb expression increased without change in cell number

claim: Expression levels of agrp1 in juvenile female medaka show no significant change according to day-length
source: We found that expression levels of neither agrp1 nor npyb show significant difference between LD and SD (Figure 4A [p=0.4179] and Figure 4B [p=0.3357]).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A with statistical significance p=0.4179

claim: Expression levels of npyb in juvenile female medaka show no significant change according to day-length
source: We found that expression levels of neither agrp1 nor npyb show significant difference between LD and SD (Figure 4A [p=0.4179] and Figure 4B [p=0.3357]).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance p=0.3357

claim: Food intake of juvenile female medaka is not different between LD and SD
source: Furthermore, food intake of juvenile female was not different between LD and SD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; p=0.7197).
evidence: Supported by food intake assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance p=0.7197

claim: agrp1 and npyb gene expression is not regulated directly by day-length itself but by LD-induced sexual maturity
source: These results suggest that neither of them is regulated directly by day-length itself. Instead, the gene expression is suggested to be regulated by LD-induced sexual maturity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that juvenile medaka do not show day-length dependent changes in agrp1 and npyb expression

claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) is the major factor important for reproduction
source: Among the ovarian estrogens, 17β-estradiol (E2) is the major factor important for reproduction (Kanda et al., 2011; Kelly and Qiu, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kanda et al., 2011; Kelly and Qiu, 2010)

claim: Blood E2 concentration of LD-conditioned female medaka is higher than those of SD
source: and the blood E2 concentration of LD-conditioned female medaka is higher than those of SD (Ikegami et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ikegami et al., 2022)

claim: Ovariectomy induces significantly lowered agrp1 expression compared to Sham
source: By using whole-brain RT-qPCR, we found that OVX induces significantly lowered agrp1 expression than Sham, and OVX+E shows a tendency to recover agrp1 expression compared with OVX (Figure 5A; Sham vs OVX: p=0.04310, OVX vs OVX+E: p=0.05790, Sham vs OVX+E: p=0.2000)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A with statistical significance p=0.04310 for Sham vs OVX

claim: OVX with E2 administration shows a tendency to recover agrp1 expression compared with OVX
source: By using whole-brain RT-qPCR, we found that OVX induces significantly lowered agrp1 expression than Sham, and OVX+E shows a tendency to recover agrp1 expression compared with OVX (Figure 5A; Sham vs OVX: p=0.04310, OVX vs OVX+E: p=0.05790, Sham vs OVX+E: p=0.2000)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A with p=0.05790 for OVX vs OVX+E (marginally significant)

claim: Ovarian E2 regulates agrp1 expression
source: which suggests that the ovarian E2 regulates agrp1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the OVX and E2 administration experiments showing changes in agrp1 expression

claim: npyb expression levels do not show significant differences among Sham, OVX, and OVX+E groups
source: On the other hand, the expression levels of npyb did not show significant differences among the three groups (Figure 5B; Sham vs OVX: p=0.1386, OVX vs OVX+E: p=0.9991, Sham vs OVX+E: p=0.08120).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B with p-values indicating no significant differences

claim: Food intake of OVX female is not significantly different between LD and SD
source: In addition, food intake of OVX female was not significantly different between LD and SD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; p=0.7308)
evidence: Supported by food intake assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance p=0.7308

claim: Medaka has three kinds of estrogen receptors: esr1, esr2a, and esr2b
source: Medaka has three kinds of estrogen receptors; esr1, esr2a, and esr2b (Tohyama et al., 2016; Kinoshita et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tohyama et al., 2016; Kinoshita et al., 2009)

claim: All three estrogen receptors have been reported to be expressed in NVT
source: and all of them have been reported to be expressed in NVT (Zempo et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Zempo et al., 2013)

claim: esr2a is co-expressed in some agrp1-expressing neurons
source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, esr2a signal was clearly co-expressed in some agrp1-expressing neurons
evidence: Supported by double in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: E2 affects the expression of agrp1 via esr2a in neurons of NVT
source: which strongly suggests that E2 affects the expression of agrp1 via esr2a in those neurons of NVT.
evidence: Inferred from the co-expression of esr2a and agrp1 in NVT neurons

claim: agrp1−/− female medaka appear skinny and have significantly lower body weight than agrp1+/+
source: As for phenotype of the knockout, the agrp1−/− female medaka appeared skinny and the body weight was significantly lower than that of agrp1+/+ (Figure 6A; body weight: p=0.04113; abdominal length: p=0.002165).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance p=0.04113

claim: Abdominal height of agrp1−/− is smaller than that of agrp1+/+
source: In addition, abdominal height of agrp1−/− was also smaller than that of agrp1+/+, while the body length was not significantly different (Figure 6A; body length: p=0.3939).
evidence: Supported by abdominal height measurements shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance p=0.002165

claim: Body length of agrp1−/− is not significantly different from agrp1+/+
source: In addition, abdominal height of agrp1−/− was also smaller than that of agrp1+/+, while the body length was not significantly different (Figure 6A; body length: p=0.3939).
evidence: Supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance p=0.3939

claim: LD agrp1−/− female medaka eat less than agrp1+/+
source: As shown in Figure 6B (p=0.004329) and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 (agrp1+/+ vs agrp1−/+: p=0.5470, agrp1+/+ vs agrp1−/−: p=0.009353, agrp1−/+ vs agrp1−/−: p=0.01234), we found that LD agrp1−/− female medaka eat less than agrp1+/+.
evidence: Supported by food intake assay data shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance p=0.004329

claim: agrp1−/− in LD condition does not show a significant increase in food intake compared with SD
source: In contrast to agrp1+/+, agrp1−/− in LD condition did not show a significant increase in food intake compared with SD (Figure 6C; p=0.5953).
evidence: Supported by food intake assay data shown in Figure 6C with statistical significance p=0.5953

claim: Pairs of agrp1−/− female and agrp1+/+ male result in fewer spawned eggs than agrp1+/+ pairs
source: Whereas the agrp1−/− females were fertile, the pairs of agrp1−/− female and agrp1+/+ male resulted in fewer spawned eggs than agrp1+/+ pairs (Figure 6D; p=0.008658).
evidence: Supported by egg spawning data shown in Figure 6D with statistical significance p=0.008658

claim: Ovarian size of agrp1−/− appears to be smaller than agrp1+/+
source: In addition, the ovarian size of agrp1−/− appeared to be smaller than agrp1+/+ (Figure 6E, left).
evidence: Supported by ovarian photographs shown in Figure 6E

claim: Gonadosomatic index (GSI) of agrp1−/− female tends to be marginally smaller than agrp1+/+
source: In particular, since relative ovarian weight normalized by body weight (gonadosomatic index [GSI]) of agrp1−/− female tended to be marginally smaller than agrp1+/+ (Figure 6E, right; p=0.06494)
evidence: Supported by GSI measurements shown in Figure 6E with p=0.06494 (marginally significant)

claim: agrp1−/− females show lower levels of expression of gonadotropin genes (fshb and lhb)
source: As shown in Figure 6F, agrp1−/− females showed lower levels of expression of gonadotropin genes (fshb and lhb; lhb: p=0.008658; fshb: p=0.02597)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F with statistical significance p=0.008658 for lhb and p=0.02597 for fshb

claim: Loss of function of agrp1 impairs breeding season-dependent feeding behavior and leads to attenuation of reproductive functions
source: which suggests that loss of function of agrp1 impaired breeding season-dependent feeding behavior and led to attenuation of reproductive functions, especially the decrease in number of spawned eggs in the breeding season.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in agrp1−/− medaka including reduced food intake and egg spawning

claim: Feeding and reproduction are closely correlated with each other
source: Feeding behavior is essential to animals for their survival and reproduction and is known to be modulated by various internal and external factors: nutritional status, sexual maturity, temperature, seasonality, etc. This behavior is known to be closely correlated with reproduction (Kauffman and Rissman, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kauffman and Rissman, 2004)

claim: Seasonal breeders show breeding season-dependent feeding behavior
source: Feeding and reproduction are known to be closely correlated with each other, and the seasonal breeders show breeding season-dependent feeding behavior.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Nutritional state modulates reproductive behaviors and functions
source: Previous studies reported that nutritional-state modulates reproductive behaviors and functions (Chen et al., 2006; Amirjani et al., 2019; Volk et al., 2017; Lynn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Chen et al., 2006; Amirjani et al., 2019; Volk et al., 2017; Lynn et al., 2010)

claim: Musk shrews show defective sexual behavior under fasted conditions
source: For example, musk shrews show defective sexual behavior under fasted conditions (Temple and Rissman, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Temple and Rissman, 2000)

claim: Fasting-induced low energy condition suppresses reproduction
source: In addition, not a few studies demonstrated that fasting-induced low energy condition suppresses reproduction (Evans and Anderson, 2012; Kalra and Kalra, 1996; Kirkwood et al., 1987; Merry and Holehan, 1979; Hasebe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Evans and Anderson, 2012; Kalra and Kalra, 1996; Kirkwood et al., 1987; Merry and Holehan, 1979; Hasebe et al., 2016)

claim: Black seabream migrates to shallow water during the breeding season where they can get more food
source: For instance, the black seabream migrates to the shallow water during the breeding season (Tsuyuki, 2018; Kawai et al., 2020) where they can get more food
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tsuyuki, 2018; Kawai et al., 2020)

claim: White-tailed deer spends more time for feeding under reproductive status
source: and the white-tailed deer spends more time for feeding under reproductive status (Stone et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Stone et al., 2017)

claim: Most model animals do not have well-defined breeding season
source: One possible reason is that most of the model animals appear to have lost the well-defined breeding season.
evidence: Stated as general knowledge about model animals

claim: Mice, rats, and zebrafish have reproductive cycles of about 4–5 days but do not have definite breeding seasonality
source: Although the mammalian models, mice and rats, and teleost model zebrafish, have reproductive cycles of about 4–5 days (Nilsson et al., 2015; Peute et al., 1978), they do not have definite breeding seasonality.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Nilsson et al., 2015; Peute et al., 1978)

claim: Medaka's reproductive status can be experimentally controlled by day-length
source: Medaka is a useful model animal, whose reproductive status can be experimentally controlled by day-length (Robinson and Rugh, 1943; Egami, 1954)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Robinson and Rugh, 1943; Egami, 1954)

claim: In long-day (LD) condition, female medaka becomes reproductive and regularly spawns every day
source: In the long-day (LD) condition (14 h light/10 h dark), female medaka becomes reproductive and regularly spawns every day
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about medaka reproductive biology

claim: In short-day (SD) condition, female medaka becomes non-reproductive
source: while it becomes non-reproductive in the short-day (SD) condition (10 h light/14 h dark).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about medaka reproductive biology

claim: Neuropeptides such as AgRP and NPY are involved in the control of feeding in mammals
source: These studies reported that some neuropeptides, such as agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and neuropeptide Y (NPY), are involved in the control of feeding and called 'feeding-related peptides' as key molecules for the regulation of feeding behavior (Hahn et al., 1998; Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011; Andermann and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hahn et al., 1998; Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011; Andermann and Lowell, 2017)

claim: Teleosts possess a regulatory mechanism for feeding similar to mammals
source: Teleosts have also been thought to possess a regulatory mechanism for feeding similar to mammals.
evidence: Stated as general knowledge in the field

claim: Expression of homologous genes coding for feeding-related peptides have been reported in teleosts
source: In fact, expression of homologous genes coding for feeding-related peptides have been reported (Rønnestad et al., 2017; Conde-Sieira and Soengas, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Rønnestad et al., 2017; Conde-Sieira and Soengas, 2016)

claim: Administration of some feeding-related peptides have been suggested to induce feeding behavior in teleosts
source: On the other hand, although administration of some of them have been suggested to induce feeding behavior in teleosts as well (Rønnestad et al., 2017), their functions in feeding behaviors still remain unclear.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Rønnestad et al., 2017)

claim: Female medaka clearly show seasonal changes in breeding conditions by day length under fixed appropriate temperature
source: In the present study, to understand mechanisms of breeding season-dependent feeding behavior, we focused on female medaka, which clearly show seasonal changes in breeding conditions by day length (Mitani et al., 2010; Kanda et al., 2008) under the fixed appropriate temperature.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Mitani et al., 2010; Kanda et al., 2008)

claim: Overall, 1025 genes showed significantly different expression between LD and SD female medaka
source: Overall, 1025 genes showed significantly different expression between LD and SD female medaka.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis results

claim: Medaka has two agrp paralogues, agrp1 and agrp2, which arose from third round whole genome duplication early in the teleost lineage
source: Medaka has two agrp paralogues, agrp1 and agrp2, and two npy paralogues, npya and npyb, which arose from third round whole genome duplication early in the teleost lineage (Liu et al., 2019; Sundström et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Liu et al., 2019; Sundström et al., 2008)

claim: Medaka has two npy paralogues, npya and npyb, which arose from third round whole genome duplication early in the teleost lineage
source: Medaka has two agrp paralogues, agrp1 and agrp2, and two npy paralogues, npya and npyb, which arose from third round whole genome duplication early in the teleost lineage (Liu et al., 2019; Sundström et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Liu et al., 2019; Sundström et al., 2008)

claim: agrp1- and npyb-expressing neurons are distributed in local brain regions
source: We found that agrp1- and npyb-expressing neurons are distributed in local brain regions (Figure 2A, B and E)
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2A, B and E

claim: npya- and agrp2-expressing neurons are more widely distributed in the brain
source: while npya- and agrp2- expressing neurons are more widely distributed (Figure 2A, C and D) in the brain.
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2A, C and D

claim: NPY released from hypothalamic npy-expressing neurons controls food intake in mice
source: Since it is suggested that NPY released from hypothalamic npy-expressing neurons controls food intake in mice (Kohno and Yada, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kohno and Yada, 2012)

claim: Total number of npya-expressing neurons in the hypothalamus is significantly larger in Fed compared with FR
source: We found that the total number of npya-expressing neurons in the hypothalamus was significantly larger in Fed compared with FR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; p=0.02857).
evidence: Supported by ISH cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance p=0.02857

claim: Significant increase in npya-expressing cell number was observed in NRL and NAT but not in NVT
source: Here, significant increase in cell number was observed in nucleus recessus lateralis (NRL) (p=0.02857) and nucleus anterior tuberis (NAT) (p=0.02857), but not in NVT (p=0.1143) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by ISH cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D with statistical significance values

claim: Higher expression of agrp1 under breeding condition may be due to increase in the number of neurons expressing agrp1
source: Since the expression level of agrp1 was higher in LD than that in SD (Figure 3A), higher expression of agrp1 under the breeding condition may be due to the increase in the number of neurons expressing agrp1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both total agrp1 expression and cell number increased in LD

claim: Estrogens are abundantly released from mature ovary and play important roles in reproductive readiness and sexual behavior
source: Among various factors associated with ovarian maturity, estrogens are known to be abundantly released from mature ovary and play important roles in reproductive readiness, sexual behavior, and so on Jennings and de Lecea, 2020; Naftolin et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2007; Clarkson and Herbison, 2009; Wintermantel et al., 2006; Micevych and Meisel, 2017; Melo and Ramsdell, 2001.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jennings and de Lecea, 2020; Naftolin et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2007; Clarkson and Herbison, 2009; Wintermantel et al., 2006; Micevych and Meisel, 2017; Melo and Ramsdell, 2001)

claim: Ovarian signal may be important for breeding season-dependent feeding behavior
source: In addition, food intake of OVX female was not significantly different between LD and SD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; p=0.7308), which suggests that ovarian signal may be important for breeding season-dependent feeding behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that OVX females lose the LD/SD difference in food intake

claim: AgRP/NPY neurons are known to regulate mammal feeding behavior
source: In mice, agrp is known to be only expressed in the hypothalamus and mostly co-expressed with npy (Hahn et al., 1998), and these AgRP/NPY neurons are known to regulate mammal feeding behavior (Shutter et al., 1997; Broberger et al., 1998; Ollmann et al., 1997; Takahashi and Cone, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Shutter et al., 1997; Broberger et al., 1998; Ollmann et al., 1997; Takahashi and Cone, 2005)

claim: Leptin receptor-knockout medaka show higher food intake and higher expressions of agrp1 and npya than wild type
source: It has been reported that leptin receptor-knockout medaka show higher food intake and higher expressions of agrp1 and npya than wild type, whereas the expression of agrp2 and npyb remained to be analyzed (Chisada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Chisada et al., 2014)

claim: In zebrafish, food restriction increased agrp1 expression
source: In zebrafish, food restriction increased agrp1 (Song et al., 2003; Opazo et al., 2018) expression
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Song et al., 2003; Opazo et al., 2018)

claim: Transgenic overexpression of agrp1 caused gain of body weight in zebrafish
source: and transgenic overexpression of agrp1 caused gain of body weight (Song and Cone, 2007), as in mammals (Graham et al., 1997; Adam et al., 2002; Hahn et al., 1998; Ilnytska and Argyropoulos, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Song and Cone, 2007; Graham et al., 1997; Adam et al., 2002; Hahn et al., 1998; Ilnytska and Argyropoulos, 2008)

claim: agrp1 knockout zebrafish eat less than the wild type
source: It has also been reported that agrp1 knockout zebrafish eat less than the wild type (Shainer et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Shainer et al., 2019)

claim: Loss of AgRP in mice showed little effect on food intake
source: although loss of AgRP in mice showed little effect on food intake (Qian et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Qian et al., 2002)

claim: agrp1 regulates feeding and may act as an orexigenic factor in teleosts
source: Our present results and these previous studies strongly support that agrp1 regulates feeding and may act as an orexigenic factor in teleosts.
evidence: Inferred from the present study results combined with previous studies in zebrafish and medaka

claim: agrp2 neurons in zebrafish are distributed differently from medaka
source: On the other hand, agrp2 neurons were distributed mainly in telencephalon, and its weak expressions were also observed in the POA and the hypothalamus (Figure 2C), which is different from the results in zebrafish (Shainer et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previous study in zebrafish (Shainer et al., 2017)

claim: AgRP2 in zebrafish is suggested to play an important role in stress response, not feeding
source: and AgRP2 in zebrafish is suggested to play an important role in stress response, not feeding (Shainer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Shainer et al., 2019)

claim: agrp2 is highly probable to be involved in functions other than feeding in female medaka
source: Thus, it is highly probable that agrp2 is involved in functions other than feeding in female medaka.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of agrp2 expression changes in response to food restriction and comparison with zebrafish studies

claim: npya is expressed in multiple brain regions including hypothalamus in medaka, similar to mammals and zebrafish
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that npya is expressed in multiple brain regions including hypothalamus in medaka (Figure 2D), which is similar to mammals (Gray and Morley, 1986) and zebrafish (Yokobori et al., 2012; Jeong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by ISH data in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies (Gray and Morley, 1986; Yokobori et al., 2012; Jeong et al., 2018)

claim: npya is not co-expressed with agrp1 nor agrp2 in zebrafish
source: We also showed that npya is not co-expressed with agrp1 nor agrp2 (Figure 2F) as in the zebrafish (Jeong et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by double ISH data in Figure 2F and citation to previous study (Jeong et al., 2018)

claim: The relationship between NPY and AgRP of teleosts may be different from that of mammals
source: suggesting that the relationship between NPY and AgRP of teleosts may be different from that of mammals, in which most of the agrp-expressing neurons co-express npy (Hahn et al., 1998).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of co-expression in teleosts compared to mammals, with citation to Hahn et al., 1998

claim: npyb expression is localized in telencephalon, similar to tiger puffer
source: Moreover, the present study also showed that npyb expression is localized in telencephalon (Figure 2E), which is similar to the previous report using tiger puffer (Kamijo et al., 2011).
